title: A convergence plot asks one question: does the error fall at the rate the scheme promises?
summary: On a log-log plot the slope of error against grid spacing is the observed order of accuracy. A scheme counts as verified when that slope matches theory, so the whole job of this figure is to be compared with its reference slopes.

media.alt: Log-log plot of L1 error against grid spacing from about 0.0125 to 0.1 for three schemes, with dashed reference lines of slope one and slope two. Two of the three curves are clearly shallower than their labelled order, and one is flat near 0.2.

source.caption: Method-of-manufactured-solutions convergence
source.note: The project page describes this study as confirming the discretization. Read as drawn, the figure is a diagnostic: see 'As drawn' below. Whether the time step was refined together with the grid is not stated on the figure.

read_the_figure.question: Does the numerical error shrink at the theoretical rate when the grid is refined?
read_the_figure.axes: x: grid spacing, Δx, on a log scale (coarse on the right, about 0.1; fine on the left, about 0.0125). y: L1 error against the manufactured solution, on a log scale. Each marker is one complete solve on one grid.
look_at: Each coloured line is one scheme. The legend gives the order the scheme is designed to have: (O2), (O1), (O2).
The two black lines are reference slopes, O(1) and O(2). They show what a straight line of that order looks like on these axes; they are not data.
Compare the slope of each coloured line with the reference line of the order in its own legend label. Parallel means the observed order equals the design order.
read_the_figure.proves: If every coloured line runs parallel to its reference line over several grid levels, the discretization is implemented as designed for this problem. That is what verification means: the code solves the equations it claims to solve, at the rate it claims.
if_wrong: A line shallower than its reference: part of the error does not shrink with Δx. Typical standard causes are a time step that was not refined with the grid, a boundary or source-term treatment of lower order, or an iterative solver stopped at a loose tolerance.
A flat line: an error floor. Something other than the spatial discretization sets the error.
A line steeper than its reference: usually too few grid levels, or a coarse grid outside the asymptotic range.
must_check: Both axes logarithmic with the same number of decades per unit length, so that slopes are comparable by eye.
At least three or four grid levels, and a constant refinement ratio.
The norm is stated (here the y-axis label says L1 error).
The observed order is printed or fitted. In this figure it is not: you have to read it off.
A floor line (round-off, time-step or tolerance floor) is drawn when the curve levels off. It is not drawn here.
as_drawn: Values below are read off the plot by eye and are approximate (about 10 percent). Grid spacings are 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125.
Diffusion/CN (blue): L1 error about 0.2 on every grid. The observed order is about 0. This is an error floor, not convergence.

AdvDiff UDS+FE (orange): about 0.033, 0.014, 0.0049, 0.0040. Orders between successive grids are about 1.2, 1.5, 0.3, and a straight-line fit over all four gives about 1.1. It follows O(1) on the coarse grids and then levels off.
AdvDiff CDS+CN (green): about 0.0245, 0.016, 0.0118, 0.0088. Successive orders are about 0.6, 0.4, 0.4, and the fit gives about 0.5, well below its labelled order of 2.

terms.meaning: A function chosen by hand, u_m(x,t), that is declared to be the exact answer. The equation's right-hand side is then computed so that u_m satisfies it exactly.
What is left over when the exact solution is substituted into the discrete equations. It is a power of the grid spacing: C h^p.
The exponent p. First order halves the error when the grid is halved; second order divides it by four.
The exponent measured from two or more actual solves. Verification compares it with the design order.
The average absolute difference between numerical and exact values over the grid points: a single number per grid.
Upwind and central differencing of the advection term. Upwind is designed first order, central second order.
Forward Euler and Crank-Nicolson time stepping. Forward Euler is first order in time, Crank-Nicolson second order.
The range of grids fine enough that the leading error term dominates. Only inside it does the slope equal the order.

remember: Verification asks 'am I solving the equations right?'. Validation asks 'am I solving the right equations?'. This figure can only speak to the first.
On log-log axes, error = C h^p is a straight line of slope p.
Observed order from two grids: p = ln(e1/e2) / ln(h1/h2).
The measured error is the sum of all error sources. The slowest-shrinking one wins as h goes to 0.
A convergence plot without printed slopes and without a floor line is incomplete.

steps.title: Choose the answer first, then make the problem fit it
steps.note: This is the manufactured-solution idea in the smallest example. Any smooth u_m works; the source term is whatever makes it exact. Checked symbolically.

steps.title: The discrete error is a power of the spacing
steps.note: For small enough h the leading truncation term dominates. C depends on derivatives of the solution, p on the scheme.

steps.title: Why central differencing is second order
steps.note: Taylor expansion of both neighbours; the even terms cancel. The leading error is proportional to h^2, so p = 2.

steps.title: Why backward (upwind) differencing is first order
steps.note: Only one neighbour is used, so the h^2 terms do not cancel and the leading error is proportional to h. For advection this error looks like extra diffusion.

steps.title: Taking logs turns the power law into a line
steps.note: So on log-log axes the slope of the error curve is p and C only shifts the line up or down. That is why the slope, not the height, is compared with theory.

steps.title: Observed order from two grids
steps.note: With a refinement ratio of two (as in this figure) the observed order is just the base-2 logarithm of the error ratio.

steps.title: Several error sources add
steps.note: If the time step is held fixed while h shrinks, the second term does not change: the curve flattens onto the floor C_t Δt^q. A flat or levelling-off curve is the typical signature, and it is why a convergence study must refine time and space together (or make the time error negligible).

steps.title: Drawing a reference line
steps.note: A line of slope p through any chosen point (h0, e0). The two black lines in the figure are this with p = 1 and p = 2, placed below the data so they do not hide it.

worked.title: Observed order of the upwind curve, between the two coarsest grids
worked.problem: Reading the orange curve: e(0.1) is about 0.033 and e(0.05) is about 0.014. What is the observed order?

solution.text: Take the base-2 logarithm of the error ratio.

worked.answer: About 1.2: close to the designed first order, given that the values were read by eye.

analyze.q: The blue curve is labelled (O2) but sits at an almost constant error. List three different things that could produce a flat curve, and say which extra run would separate them.
analyze.hint: Refine only the time step; tighten the solver tolerance; change the boundary treatment.

analyze.q: The orange curve follows slope 1 for two refinements and then levels off. Is that evidence that the scheme is first order, evidence that it is not, or neither? What would you do next?
analyze.hint: Think about the asymptotic range and about a floor entering at fine grids.

analyze.q: The green curve is labelled (O2) but its fitted slope is about 0.5. Which two of the error terms in the 'several error sources add' step could explain a slope between the time order and the space order?

evaluate.q: Would you sign off on this code as verified from this figure alone? State the minimum extra evidence you would need.
evaluate.hint: Orders printed, a floor line, the time step used, and a run where only one error source is active.

evaluate.q: The reference lines are drawn well below the data. Does that change what the figure can prove? Where should they go instead?
evaluate.hint: Slopes are what matter, but lines placed through the first data point make the comparison immediate.

create: Redraw this figure so that it passes the F5.1 checklist: fitted slopes in the legend, a dotted floor line, and the time step stated in the title.
Design a three-run study that separates spatial and temporal error for the Crank-Nicolson / central scheme: which two things do you hold fixed, and which one do you vary?

checks.hint: What does error = C h^p become after taking logs?
checks.answer: Because a power law becomes a straight line there: ln e = ln C + p ln h. The slope is the order p, so orders can be compared by eye and the constant C only shifts the line.

checks.q: An error falls from 4.0e-3 to 1.0e-3 when the grid is halved. What is the observed order?
checks.hint: Use the base-2 logarithm of the ratio.
checks.answer: The ratio is 4, so p = log2(4) = 2: second order.

checks.q: A convergence curve is straight with slope 2 on the coarse grids and then goes flat. What does the flat part tell you?
checks.hint: Which term in the error sum does not depend on h?
checks.answer: That another error source, one that does not shrink with h (a time-step, tolerance or round-off floor), has overtaken the spatial error. The scheme can still be second order; the floor hides it.

checks.q: Two curves have the same slope but one lies ten times higher. Which scheme is better?
checks.hint: Slope is the order; height is C.
checks.answer: The lower one is more accurate on these grids, but they have the same order. Order tells how fast error falls with refinement, C tells how large it is to begin with. Which is 'better' depends on the grids you can afford.

checks.q: How would you manufacture a solution for advection-diffusion u_t + a u_x = nu u_xx?
checks.hint: Pick u_m, then compute the residual of the PDE.
checks.answer: Choose a smooth u_m(x,t), for example a product of a sine in x and an exponential in t, compute f = (u_m)_t + a (u_m)_x - nu (u_m)_xx symbolically, add f as a source term to the solver, and use u_m for the initial and boundary data. The solver's error against u_m is then exactly its discretization error.
